scenario: AITA for telling my sister that her beating breast cancer was not impressive and not inspirational? | Three years ago my older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Within six months her cancer was cleared. She had minor radiAtion and then hormone therapy afterwards. She is 100% fine and healthy no need for surgery. We all came together and supported her during this time. Now, the thing has been is that she hasn’t stopped to remind us constantly about how she is a cancer survivor. And has made it her identity. She has since plastered it all over social media. I don’t mind it because I can choose to ignore it. But this holiday season she was insufferable. My breaking point happened when my dad who has been dealing with nerve problems was telling us how physical therapy wasn’t working for him and he will likely need to get surgery. My sister started bringing up her cancer story again. I snapped and told her that her surviving breast cancer was not impressive nor inspiration, it has a survival rate of 96% and to stop making everything about her story. My sister walked out of the room. I thought my family would back me up but instead my parents backed up my sister. My dad didn’t say anything but he was on my sisters side. I don’t know maybe what I said wasn’t the nicest way but I don’t think I was wrong in what I said.

prediction.raw: 1 I think you were wrong in what you said, and here's why: while it's true that the survival rate for breast cancer is high, especially with early detection and treatment, that doesn't diminish the personal struggle and emotional toll that your sister went through. Cancer diagnosis and treatment can be a life-altering experience, and it's natural for your sister to feel proud of her resilience and want to share her story. Moreover, your sister's experience is not just about the statistics; it's about her personal journey, her fears, her struggles, and her triumphs. By minimizing her experience and telling her that it's not impressive or inspirational, you came across as insensitive and dismissive of her feelings. It's also worth considering the context in which you made your comment. Your dad was sharing his struggles with nerve problems, and your sister was trying to offer a message of hope and resilience. Instead of being supportive, you snapped at her and made her feel belittled. While it's understandable that you might feel frustrated with your sister's constant reminders about her cancer experience, there are kinder and more empathetic ways to address the issue. You could have had a private conversation with her, expressing your feelings and concerns in a non-confrontational way. By doing so, you might have avoided hurting her feelings and causing a rift in your family. In hindsight, it's not about whether your sister's experience was "impressive" or "inspirational" to you; it's about being supportive and understanding of her feelings and experiences. Your parents' reaction suggests that they value empathy and kindness, and it's something to consider in your future interactions with your sister.
